record.title: Untrusted caller name is concatenated into SQL passed to db.query
record.description: The lower-trust principal is the host's caller. README.md states that values under request.query come from that caller and that this library does not trust them. handleLookup accepts that request. When request.query has no own id property, line 23 passes request.query.name to findUserByName. findUserByName places name between single quotes in SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE name = '...' and passes that string as the only argument to db.query. The crossed boundary is that untrusted name becoming SQL statement text for the users lookup. README.md states that db.query sends its first argument to a SQL engine and that a second argument, when present, is the bound parameter list. This call passes no second argument. The strongest source-visible control is the own-property test on id: it selects findUserById, whose statement text is constant and whose second argument is [id], only when id is an own property. That test does not bind or escape name. findUserByName is exported, so the same concatenation is reachable without the id test. The concrete result still requiring a local observation is the argument list db.query receives for a name containing one single quote: the quote is inside the statement text and no bound-parameter array is present.
record.claimed_root_cause: findUserByName concatenates the caller-supplied name into SQL statement text and calls db.query with that text as its only argument, so the name is not a bound parameter.

trace.description: When request.query has no own id property, handleLookup passes request.query.name, which README.md says comes from the host's caller and is untrusted, to findUserByName.
findUserByName concatenates name between single quotes into the SQL statement text.
db.query receives that statement as its only argument, which is the argument README.md says is sent to a SQL engine.

evidence.description: The SQL text is built by concatenating the name argument between single quotes.
db.query is called with that SQL text and no bound-parameter array.
The strongest source-visible control is this own-property test. It selects findUserById only when id is present and leaves the name path concatenated.
findUserById passes a constant SQL string and the array [id].
handleLookup passes request.query.name into findUserByName when id is not an own property of request.query.
findUserByName is exported, so a host can call the concatenation without the id test in handleLookup.
Values under request.query come from the host's caller, and the library does not trust them.
db.query sends its first argument to a SQL engine. When a second argument is present, that array is the bound parameter list.

blockers: The missing fact is the local SQL result: there is no observed argument list for db.query when handleLookup is called with a request.query that has no own id property and a name containing one single quote. Sandbox execution is not approved. A read-only bind mount worked and a network namespace blocked a ping, but scratch-only writes are not enforced, a loop mount failed, and cgroup limits are unavailable, so this run cannot produce that bounded local result.

validation_plan.local: In an approved sandbox with a read-only target, scratch-only writes, and enforced resource limits, load src/library.js and call handleLookup with a db.query that records its arguments and returns a dummy value, using request.query set to an object whose only own field is name and whose name contains one single quote. Record the argument list and stop. The concrete result to capture is whether the sole argument contains that quote inside the statement text and no bound-parameter array is present. Do not open a database connection or send the statement to a SQL engine.
